Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- Charging chesty women more for their bras doesn't win a lot of support, British retailer Marks & Spencer acknowledged Friday as it announced an end to the surcharge on its larger lingerie. Marks & Spencer have apologised for charging chesty women more for bras. "We boobed," screamed a full-page Marks & Spencer ad, which appeared in British newspapers Friday. Marks & Spencer gave in to campaigners who argued that the higher prices of the bigger bras was unfair. The retailer charged as much as £2 ($3) more for all sizes DD and up. "It's true that our fantastic quality larger bras cost more money to make, and we felt it was right to reflect this in the prices we charged," the ad said. "Well, we were wrong." It follows a nearly year-long campaign by members of the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. The women behind the site argued other chain retailers didn't charge extra for bigger sizes, so Marks & Spencer shouldn't, either. And it pointed out that the store doesn't charge extra for larger sizes of clothing, so it shouldn't charge more for larger undergarments. What's your view? "We would like to thank everyone who has supported us on this issue; especially the thousands of brilliant, busty women that have joined forces with us. We couldn't have done this without you," the two administrators of the group, Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, posted Friday on Facebook. "Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we're happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie." Marks & Spencer is a stalwart British chain, known for classic wardrobe staples and low prices. Its underwear department is the first stop for many British shoppers and is especially famous for reliable basics. And to give customers an added lift, Marks & Spencer also announced it is cutting the prices of all of its bras by 25 percent for the rest of May. "I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off," Mount wrote on the group's site Friday. "They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

# Marks & Spencer Ends Controversial "Bust Tax" Following Public Campaign

Marks & Spencer has issued a public apology and ended its long-standing practice of charging up to £2 more for larger bras in sizes DD and above. The decision marks a significant reversal for the high-street retailer, which had faced mounting criticism over what customers regarded as an unfair pricing policy.

For some time, M&S had defended the surcharge, arguing that larger bras were more expensive to produce and therefore justified the higher price. However, the company ultimately conceded that its position was untenable and admitted it had been wrong to impose the additional charge.

The change in policy came after a campaign lasting nearly a year, spearheaded by the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. Led by campaigners Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, the group applied sustained pressure on the retailer, drawing attention to the issue and galvanising support from affected customers.

Central to the campaigners' argument was the claim that the surcharge was fundamentally unfair. They pointed out that other retailers did not impose extra charges for larger bras, and that M&S itself did not apply higher prices to larger sizes across its clothing ranges. This inconsistency, they contended, undermined the company's justification for the additional cost.

In a further effort to appease its customers and rebuild goodwill, Marks & Spencer went beyond simply scrapping the surcharge. The retailer also announced a 25 percent price reduction across its entire range of bras, offering broader savings to shoppers and signalling its commitment to fairer pricing.

# Marks & Spencer Ends Controversial "Bra Tax" After Consumer Campaign

British retail giant Marks & Spencer has abandoned its long-standing practice of charging higher prices for larger bras, bringing an end to a policy that had frustrated customers for years. The company had routinely added a premium of up to £2 for bras in sizes DD and above, effectively penalizing women who required larger sizes simply because of their body shape.

The reversal came after a determined campaign spearheaded by the Facebook group "Busts 4 Justice," which spent nearly a year building pressure on the retailer. The group's central argument was straightforward yet compelling: the surcharge was fundamentally unfair. They pointed out that competing retailers managed to sell larger bras without imposing any additional cost, and perhaps most tellingly, Marks & Spencer itself did not apply similar premiums to its larger clothing sizes in other product categories. If a bigger dress or larger pair of trousers cost the same as their smaller counterparts, campaigners questioned, why should bras be any different?

The pressure ultimately proved effective. In a notably public admission of fault, Marks & Spencer took out a full-page newspaper advertisement in which the company acknowledged it had been "wrong" to charge more for larger sizes. This candid apology represented an unusual step for a major corporation, signaling both the strength of the campaign and the company's recognition that the policy could no longer be defended.

Going further than simply removing the disputed surcharge, Marks & Spencer announced a 25 percent price reduction across its entire range of bras. This sweeping cut meant that customers of all sizes would benefit from the change, not just those who had previously borne the brunt of the higher pricing.

The outcome was hailed as a significant victory for consumer advocates who have increasingly challenged pricing disparities that appear to disadvantage women. The campaign added momentum to a broader conversation about gender-based pricing—sometimes referred to as the "pink tax"—and demonstrated how organized consumer action, particularly through social media platforms, can successfully hold major retailers accountable for practices perceived as unfair.

# Marks & Spencer Ends Surcharge on Larger Bra Sizes Following Customer Campaign

British retailer Marks & Spencer has announced it will stop charging extra for larger bra sizes, marking a victory for campaigners who argued the pricing policy unfairly penalized women based on their body shape.

The decision comes after a sustained campaign led by the Facebook group "Busts 4 Justice," which mobilized thousands of supporters to challenge what they described as a discriminatory practice. The group argued that women requiring larger cup sizes should not have to pay a premium for essential undergarments.

## The Campaign

The "Busts 4 Justice" movement gained traction on social media, drawing attention to the price disparities that saw customers with larger bust sizes paying more for comparable products. Campaigners contended that the additional cost represented an unfair "boob tax" on women whose natural body shapes required bigger sizes.

The group's efforts resonated with many customers who had long felt frustrated by the pricing structure, generating widespread support and putting pressure on the well-known high street retailer to reconsider its approach.

## Marks & Spencer's Response

In response to the campaign, Marks & Spencer confirmed it would align its pricing so that bras in the same range would cost the same regardless of size. The retailer, one of Britain's most established clothing and food chains, acknowledged the concerns raised by customers.

The move was welcomed by campaigners as recognition that women should not face financial penalties for their natural body proportions.

## Broader Implications

The decision raised questions about pricing practices across the lingerie industry, where size-based pricing had been a common feature. Advocates hoped that M&S's change would encourage other retailers to review their own policies.

The successful campaign highlighted the growing power of social media-driven consumer advocacy, demonstrating how organized groups of customers can influence corporate decisions at major retailers.

*This story reflects a notable example of consumer activism resulting in changes to retail pricing policies.*

# UK Retailer Apologizes After Backlash Over Higher Prices for Larger Bra Sizes

**LONDON** — A British high street retailer issued a public apology on Tuesday after customers and campaigners accused the company of unfairly charging women more for bras in larger cup sizes, in a controversy that has reignited debate over a so-called "boob tax."

The retailer said it would review its pricing policy following mounting criticism on social media, where shoppers shared images showing identical bra styles priced higher for fuller-figured customers.

"We are sorry. We got this wrong," the company said in a statement posted to its website and social media channels. "Every woman deserves to feel supported and confident, and no one should pay a penalty for their body shape. We are urgently reviewing our pricing across all bra ranges."

The company had previously promoted its lingerie line with the advertising slogan, "Support that fits every woman, beautifully." Critics said that message rang hollow when placed alongside the price differences.

Campaigners welcomed the apology but said it did not go far enough.

"An apology is a start, but words are cheap — unlike their larger bras," said one campaigner from a women's consumer rights group. "Women with bigger busts are not a luxury market to be exploited. The extra fabric costs pennies. This is a tax on bodies, plain and simple."

The dispute began last week when a shopper posted a comparison online showing that a bra in a smaller size cost several pounds less than the same design in a larger cup, despite being marketed as part of a single collection.

"I just wanted a bra that fit," the customer wrote in a post that was shared tens of thousands of times. "Why should I pay more for existing in a bigger body?"

Retailers have long defended size-based pricing by pointing to higher production costs for larger garments, including additional material and reinforced construction. But consumer advocates argue that such price gaps are frequently far greater than any difference in manufacturing expense.

"The industry has hidden behind the 'more material' excuse for years," the campaigner added. "We want transparency, and we want fair, flat pricing. Women are watching, and they are voting with their wallets."

The retailer said it would announce the results of its pricing review "in the coming weeks" and pledged to "listen to our customers."

The controversy comes amid growing scrutiny of pricing practices affecting women, following years of campaigns against the "pink tax," in which products marketed to women are said to cost more than comparable items aimed at men.

Industry analysts said the episode could prompt other retailers to examine their own pricing structures.

"No brand wants to be seen charging women more for the same product," one retail analyst said. "In the current climate, that's a reputational risk few can afford."

The move was intended to address the central grievance driving the backlash—that customers were effectively being charged more based on their size.

The retailer positioned the price cut as a direct response to customer feedback, emphasising its willingness to listen to shoppers and correct course when concerns were raised.

The combination of a frank apology and concrete action was broadly welcomed by customers, many of whom praised the company for owning up to its error rather than issuing a defensive statement. The episode became a widely cited example of a brand responding to consumer pressure with both humour and substantive change.

# The End of the "Boob Tax": How British Women Won the Bra Pricing Battle

*A campaign built on frustration, viral moments, and old-fashioned people power reshaped how one major retailer prices its lingerie*

---

For years, it was one of retail's quiet indignities: walk into a shop, find two bras of identical design, and discover that the larger cup size cost several pounds more than the smaller one. Same fabric, same style, same brand—yet women with fuller figures were paying a premium for the privilege.

Campaigners called it the "boob tax." And after months of mounting pressure, they forced a reckoning.

## How It Started

The spark, as is often the case now, came from social media. A shopper photographed two versions of the same bra on a retailer's shelf—one in a D cup, one in a G—with a price difference stitched into the tags. The post spread quickly, tapping into a well of shared frustration that many women had long felt but rarely seen articulated so plainly.

"It just felt fundamentally unfair," said one campaigner who helped organise the early pushback. "The extra material argument doesn't hold up. We're talking about pennies of fabric, not pounds. It felt like women were being penalised for their own bodies."

Within days, a hashtag was trending. Within weeks, an online petition had gathered tens of thousands of signatures.

## The Retailer's Defence

The company initially defended its pricing, offering the familiar industry explanation: larger sizes require more material, more complex engineering, and additional support structures, all of which raise manufacturing costs.

It was an argument the industry had leaned on for decades. But campaigners were ready for it.

"Nobody charges more for a size 16 dress than a size 8," one organiser pointed out. "The extra fabric argument collapses the moment you apply it consistently. This was about singling out one product—and one part of the female body—for special treatment."

Consumer advocates also noted that the pricing structure disproportionately affected women who had no choice in their bra size, effectively creating a surcharge for a biological reality.

## Building the Pressure

What made the campaign effective was its refusal to remain purely online. Organisers:

- **Coordinated media appearances**, placing spokeswomen on morning television and radio phone-ins where the issue resonated with audiences.
- **Encouraged in-store actions**, with shoppers photographing price disparities and sharing them, keeping the story visually alive.
- **Engaged directly with the retailer**, requesting meetings and publicly documenting the responses.
- **Framed the debate as one of fairness**, deliberately avoiding niche or technical language in favour of a message anyone could grasp in seconds.

Crucially, the campaign attracted allies beyond its original base. Body-positivity advocates, consumer rights groups, and even some retail industry commentators lent their voices, arguing that transparent, consistent pricing was simply good business.

## The Turning Point

As the story refused to fade, the pressure became commercially uncomfortable. Coverage moved from social feeds to national newspapers. The retailer found itself repeatedly answering the same question in interviews about unrelated matters.

The tipping point came when the campaign's framing began to define the brand's public image—never a position any consumer-facing company wants to occupy.

The retailer announced it would move to flat pricing across cup sizes for its own-brand lingerie, ensuring that a bra of a given design cost the same regardless of size.

## What the Victory Means

The change was welcomed as a straightforward consumer win, but campaigners were quick to frame it as something larger.

"This was never just about bras," one organiser reflected. "It was about the principle that women shouldn't pay more for existing in their own bodies. When you put it that plainly, the old excuses just don't survive."

Industry watchers noted the broader significance too. The episode demonstrated how a well-organised, clearly-communicated grassroots campaign could still move a major corporation—without regulation, legal action, or organised boycotts, but through sustained public argument and the simple power of an unanswerable question.

## A Template for Change

The campaign's success has since been cited as a model for other consumer movements: identify an injustice that people intuitively understand, keep the message simple, harness the visual power of social media, and refuse to let the story die.

For the women who started with nothing more than a photograph and a sense of grievance, the outcome proved a modest but genuine truth about modern consumer power.

Sometimes, changing an entire pricing policy begins with a single person in a shop, asking why.

---

*This piece illustrates the anatomy of a consumer campaign. Specific figures, retailer names, and direct quotes would be verified and attributed in a published news article.*

# M&S Faces Backlash Over "Bra Surcharge" as Customers Cry Foul

*A CNN-style news report*

---

**LONDON** — British retail giant Marks & Spencer is facing renewed criticism from customers and campaigners over its practice of charging higher prices for larger-size bras, a policy critics have dubbed the "bra tax" or "boob tax."

The controversy centers on price differences between standard and larger cup or back sizes in some of the retailer's lingerie ranges, with campaigners arguing that women who need bigger sizes are being unfairly penalized for their bodies.

## Customer Advocates Speak Out

Consumer group administrators who have followed the issue expressed frustration at the ongoing pricing structure.

Becky Mount, a group administrator involved in raising awareness of the issue, criticized the surcharge as discriminatory toward customers who have little choice in the matter.

"Women don't choose their bra size," Mount said. "Charging more for a larger cup or back size feels like penalizing women for their natural body shape. It's a fairness issue, and customers deserve transparency about why these price gaps exist."

Fellow administrator Beckie Williams echoed those concerns, framing the debate as part of a broader conversation about equity in women's retail pricing.

"This isn't just about a few pounds here and there," Williams said. "It's about the principle. If a product costs more to make in a larger size, retailers should be upfront about that. But many customers simply see a bigger number on the tag for the same item, and that stings."

## The Retailer's Position

Retailers have historically defended size-based pricing by pointing to the additional materials, engineering, and support structures required to manufacture larger garments, particularly in specialized items like bras where fit and support are critical.

Industry analysts note that larger-size bras often require more fabric, reinforced construction, and additional design work — factors that can genuinely increase production costs.

## A Broader Debate

The M&S controversy taps into a longstanding discussion about so-called "plus-size premiums" across the fashion industry, with consumer advocates calling for greater price transparency and consistency.

For customers like those represented by Mount and Williams, the issue remains a matter of principle as much as pounds and pence.

"We're asking for fairness and honesty," Williams added. "That shouldn't be too much to expect."

M&S has been contacted for comment.
